title: Criticism That Lands: Give High Standards and Trust First
dek: Criticism is accepted not because you soften it with praise, but because the other person sees: the bar is high, and you believe they can reach it. In the experiment, a single sentence — "the standards are high, but I believe you can meet them" — drove Black students' revision rates to the highest.
why: The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism and turns the intervention into a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of dense information, no generic communication platitudes.
who: Managers, teachers, and HR professionals who need to deliver negative feedback to subordinates, students, or colleagues from different backgrounds; also those in diverse teams who often worry about being stereotyped.

points.h: Identity bias makes people choke in the moment
points.body: When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and the situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. This worry comes from the situation itself; it immediately depresses performance on tests, sports, or intellectual tasks, and over time makes people avoid such situations, shaping who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety comes not from ability but from the expectation of being defined by a label.

points.h: Social media makes labels surround and pursue you
points.body: Social media's power lies in rapidly spreading caricatures of groups; people have no patience for nuance or exceptions, so it naturally multiplies situations where you feel "I'll be seen through my identity." It occasionally spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone is negative. The result: in a diverse society, everyone is more vigilant about their identity and what others might think.

In racially integrated classrooms, Black students constantly worry about being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about what they value most in life. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the opportunity to signal to the teacher "I'm more than that label," and their grades began to rise, entering a positive feedback loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → even better grades. The intervention costs almost nothing yet changes long-term trajectories.

points.h: In diverse settings, the vigilance: remember or forget
points.body: The author calls this state churn. When people from different backgrounds work together and the stakes are high, you oscillate between two choices: remember "others may interpret me through my group's stereotype" to protect yourself, or forget it and relax into trusting the people in front of you. This isn't fragility; it's real situational pressure. When the stakes are high, it constantly drains attention that should go to the task.

points.h: High standards plus trust make feedback work
points.body: In an experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Two delivery methods — direct feedback, or a "positive high hat" first — were trusted by white students but highly distrusted by Black students. A third method added just one sentence: "We have high standards because the essay will be published; I've read your essay and believe you can meet them." Under this condition, Black students took the essay home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

points.h: Don't assume others already trust you
points.body: Having served as dean and provost for years, Claude believes the most useful ability is realizing that every person you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, but in reality, others worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders excel at sending this signal first: even if employees disagree with a decision, if they feel respected as people and for their potential, the team atmosphere changes completely.

points.h: Let people see you as human before talking trust
points.body: Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what the situation means to them; when power is unequal, the higher-status person must release safety signals first. Second, near-paranoid clarity — beating around the bush destroys valuable information. Third, warmth and goodwill — people need to confirm you are a good person before they hand over trust. Matt summarizes it as connection, clarity, and care.

terms.def: The situational pressure of being distracted and underperforming in important settings due to fear of being judged by a negative stereotype about your group.
The author's coinage: the vigilance and anxiety felt in diverse settings with high stakes, from worrying about being devalued based on identity.
To stop regarding academics or career as part of one's self-worth in order to escape persistent stereotype pressure.

facts.k: Black students' rate of taking the essay home to revise
facts.v: three times that of other experimental conditions

facts.k: Duration of the self-reflection writing exercise
